What Dr. Kemp says to focus on Built from Dr. Walter Kemp's Cystic and Congenital Diseases of the Kidney Parts 1–2 (slides + narration). Part 1 objectives: hydronephrosis; simple vs acquired cysts; ADPKD and ARPKD (etiology, epidemiology, presentation, pathology). Part 2: morphology of congenital anomalies, Potter sequence, ureter anomalies, and clinical presentation. His references are Robbins Basic Pathology; he says to not memorize exact incidence numbers (sources disagree) and that purple text on his slides means "don't memorize." Practice questions sit at the end of each section; the summary table is last. beyond source = standard teaching I added; corrected = source slip fixed.

1. Hydronephrosis

  • Not a cystic disease (he includes it because the dilated spaces look cystic). It is a general reaction to obstruction.
  • Definition: local or generalized dilation of the renal pelvis and/or calyceal system.
  • Cause: obstruction of urine flow, so urine backs up into the kidney. Examples he gives: a stone in part of the calyceal system, or obstruction at the pelvis outlet, along the ureter, or at the ureter-bladder junction.
  • Focal vs generalized: obstruction of part of the calyceal system dilates only that part; obstruction at the pelvis outlet or ureter dilates the whole kidney.
  • Gross: dilated pelvis and calyces with thinning (atrophy) of the overlying cortex from pressure. In his example the space is filled with fat as the parenchyma atrophies.
  • Microscopic: nonspecific, such as fibrosis, inflammation, thinned parenchyma, globally sclerotic glomeruli.
Hydronephrosis: dilated pelvis and calyces (yellow arrows) with a thin overlying cortex.

2. Simple Cyst vs Acquired Cystic Disease

  • Simple cyst = fluid-filled sac, almost always in the cortex (rarely medulla). Very common at autopsy and more frequent with age; he thinks of an obstructed tubule filling with fluid.
  • Mostly asymptomatic; rupture can cause flank pain.
  • Wall should be paper thin (see-through), with no solid or papillary areas.
  • Any solidity must be worked up for renal cell carcinoma, which can be very cystic (he has seen a huge cystic mass with a small solid edge that was RCC).
Simple cyst: a sac of fluid with no solid or papillary areas on the inner surface.
Simple cystAcquired cystic disease
CauseSporadic, with agingDialysis
RCC riskNot a risk factorRisk factor for RCC
ClinicalUsually silent; pain if rupturedKidneys of long-term dialysis patients

3. Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)

Source gapThe first ADPKD slide (genetics, epidemiology, clinical features) is not in the PDF. This section uses his narration for those points; the pathology slide text is from the PDF.

Genetics and pathogenesis

  • PKD1 (~85–90%) or PKD2 (much less). He cautions against memorizing exact numbers, but PKD1 is the more common (a possible exam question).
  • Both gene products sit together on the cilia and act as one protein complex, so a mutation in either gene gives the same phenotype.
  • Result: increased cell production and increased fluid secretion from the cells → cysts.
  • Common: 1 in 200–1000; about 5% of ESRD.
Beyond source beyond sourcePKD1 encodes polycystin-1 and PKD2 encodes polycystin-2; PKD1 disease usually reaches ESRD earlier. Neither was stated in the slides.

Presentation

  • Usually third to fifth decade: born with it, but the kidney has huge reserve (half of one kidney can clear blood). Dominant diseases have variable expression, so age at presentation varies.
  • Hypertension, hematuria (cyst hemorrhage), proteinuria, urinary tract infection, flank pain or pressure from an abdominal mass (kidneys can reach 1–3 kg), stones (supersaturation), sterile pyuria, renal failure.
  • Enlarged kidneys can compress the renal artery or ureter.
  • Key association: berry aneurysm and ruptured berry aneurysm → subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Pathology

  • Gross: enlarged kidneys, >50 cysts, often so cystic that the normal parenchyma is obscured. With a known family history, a few cysts at a young age can be enough for the diagnosis.
  • Microscopic: some normal parenchyma (tubules, glomeruli) between the cysts.
ADPKD: massively enlarged kidneys replaced by cysts; cut section (inset).
Enlarged ADPKD kidneys, and subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

4. Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease (ARPKD)

  • PKHD1 mutation encoding fibrocystin, on cilia, involved in cell differentiation, proliferation and adhesion. Mnemonic: "H" goes with recessive (PKHD1).
  • Associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis.
  • Much less common than ADPKD. Reported incidence ranges widely (1 in 20,000 in Robbins; 6,000–140,000 in Rubin; 6,000–40,000 in Becker and Avner), which is why he says exact numbers are not worth memorizing.
  • Bimodal presentation: infants (most) and early adulthood. About 70% of children have a palpable mass by 1 month.
  • Collecting duct involvement → decreased urine concentration → polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration.
  • Also: hypertension, hematuria, proteinuria, sterile pyuria.
  • Chronic renal failure: poor growth, anemia (low erythropoietin), osteodystrophy (disturbed vitamin D handling).

Pathology: cysts are in the collecting ducts only

  • Gross: kidneys enlarged but the outside looks normal (cysts are internal).
  • Microscopic: dilated collecting ducts lined up in parallel rows with spaces between, like a fan or filter.
ARPKD: cut kidney with radial cystic spaces; histology shows dilated collecting ducts (arrows).

ADPKD vs ARPKD

Common to bothEnlarged kidneys, hypertension, concentrating defect, sterile pyuria
Suggests ADPKDPositive family history; asymptomatic or late presentation; can be unilateral; extrarenal cysts; cerebral aneurysms; hematuria; UTI
Suggests ARPKDNeonatal presentation; hepatosplenomegaly; portal hypertension; bacterial cholangitis; ESRD in childhood
Becker and Avner (1995) comparison from his slide.
  • He notes hematuria can also occur in ARPKD, and that ADPKD can progress to ESRD but usually later, rarely in childhood.
  • Congenital hepatic fibrosis causes portal hypertension.
Transcript slip correctedThe auto-transcript renders "hepatic fibrosis" and "ARPKD" erratically ("congenital paddock fibrosis," "awesome recessive"). The terms are congenital hepatic fibrosis and autosomal recessive PKD.

5. Medullary Cystic Diseases

He says the terminology is not always clear. Don't worry about the gene lists.

DiseaseKey points
Medullary sponge kidneyCystic collecting ducts; innocuous (no progressive renal failure). The one in his autopsy example; the most common of the group
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (old name: medullary cystic kidney disease)Adults; progressive renal failure; no definitive mechanism. Genes: MUC1 (mucin-1, distal nephron), UMOD (uromodulin, thick ascending limb), REN (prorenin, JGA)
NephronophthisisSmall cysts at the corticomedullary junction; no increase in kidney size. Most common cause of ESRD in children (infantile, juvenile, adolescent forms). Polyuria/polydipsia, sodium wasting, tubular acidosis. Can be sporadic; AD (familial juvenile nephronophthisis) or AR (renal-retinal dysplasia)
Medullary sponge kidney: involves collecting ducts.
Why is nephronophthisis hard to diagnose by biopsy?The cysts sit at the corticomedullary junction, but a needle biopsy samples mostly cortex (aimed at glomerular disease), so the cysts may be missed.
Beyond source beyond sourceNephronophthisis is usually inherited as autosomal recessive (NPHP genes), and ADTKD is the dominant disease; the slide's AD label for nephronophthisis is the less common situation.

6. Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney

AnomalyKey points
Uteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstructionBlockage where the pelvis meets the ureter; causes generalized hydronephrosis with the cortex thinned to a few millimeters
Posterior urethral valves; prune belly syndromeUrinary tract obstruction → hydronephrosis, distended bladder, atrophy of the overlying abdominal muscle (the "prune belly")
AgenesisUnilateral is compatible with life; bilateral is not
Location (ectopic / pelvic kidney)Kidney in the pelvis; often looks convoluted and malformed. (Pelvic kidneys are where transplants are placed.)
Fusion (horseshoe kidney)Fuses across the midline; associated with Turner syndrome
HypoplasiaKidney never reached normal size (vs atrophy: reached normal size, then shrank)
DysplasiaDisorganized growth. In kids it is not pre-neoplastic (in adults, dysplasia is a cancer precursor)
UPJ obstruction (yellow arrow): generalized dilation of the pelvis and calyces; cortex thinned to a few mm.
Pelvic kidney (left side; bladder at right) vs the normally placed contralateral kidney.
Horseshoe kidney: fused across the midline.
Turner syndrome recap (from his narration)Horseshoe kidney, coarctation of the aorta, short widely spaced nipples, cystic hygroma leading to neck webbing, streak ovaries and primary amenorrhea.

Hypoplasia and dysplasia

Left: bilateral cystic kidneys (hypoplastic and dysplastic), a fetal autopsy, not compatible with life. Right: unilateral renal hypoplasia in an adult, compatible with life.
Renal dysplasia: primitive mesenchyme, primitive tubules (blue arrows; not clearly proximal, distal or collecting), and a few normal glomeruli (yellow arrow).
  • Dysplasia histology: primitive mesenchymal tissue and primitive tubules, with loose myxoid fibrotic stroma; cartilage islands can appear (from his practice question).

7. Potter Sequence

  • A sequence = one pathologic lesion causes everything else (unlike a syndrome such as Down).
  • Cause: oligohydramnios due to significant fetal renal disease. Amniotic fluid is largely fetal urine, so kidneys that don't make urine leave too little fluid.
  • Features: small chest with pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies, plus limb anomalies and low-set ears (from his practice question).
  • Infants usually die early from respiratory failure due to the pulmonary hypoplasia.
  • Link to multicystic dysplastic kidney: only if it is bilateral (no urine) → oligohydramnios → Potter. Unilateral disease causes nothing because the other kidney makes urine.
Transcript slip correctedThe narration says "pulmonary hyperplasia." The slide and the pathology are pulmonary hypoplasia (small, underdeveloped lungs).
Pulmonary hypoplasia: the lung apices (white arrows) should reach the heart apex (yellow line) but are small.
Infant with Potter sequence (flat facies).
Unilateral hypoplastic and dysplastic kidney found in an adult at autopsy: no effect on function, because half of one kidney is enough.

8. Ureter Anomalies, Associated Syndromes and Presentation

Ureteral duplication

  • Incomplete duplication: bifid pelves and/or bifid ureter that join into one ureter entering the bladder.
  • Complete duplication: two separate ureters from kidney to bladder (one or both sides).

Spectrum with chromosomal syndromes (do not memorize)

SyndromeRenal findings listed
Trisomy 18 (Edwards)Horseshoe kidney, ectopic kidney, double ureter, hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney
Trisomy 13 (Patau)Polycystic kidney, hydronephrosis, horseshoe kidney, double ureter

Textbooks give a truncated list; references such as Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation show a wider range.

Clinical presentation

PresentationExamples
Asymptomatic / incidental at autopsyEctopic kidney, unilateral cystic renal dysplasia, horseshoe kidney
Mass lesionEctopic kidney, cystic renal dysplasia
Recurrent infectionsEctopic kidney (abnormal position disturbs urine flow). Recurrent UTIs in a young child should prompt a search for a structural anomaly
Progressive renal failureCystic renal dysplasia, especially if the other kidney is also diseased (hypertension, diabetes)

9. High-Yield Summary Table

ConditionKey points
HydronephrosisNot cystic. Obstruction → dilated pelvis/calyces, thin cortex; focal vs generalized by obstruction site
Simple cystSporadic, aging, cortex; thin wall; no RCC risk; any solid part → rule out RCC
Acquired cystic diseaseFrom dialysis; RCC risk
ADPKDPKD1 (more common) / PKD2; cilia; 1 in 200–1000; ~5% ESRD; adults (30s–50s); HTN, hematuria, UTI, stones, mass; berry aneurysm; huge kidneys, >50 cysts, some normal parenchyma
ARPKDPKHD1 (fibrocystin); infants; congenital hepatic fibrosis → portal HTN, cholangitis; collecting duct cysts, normal external surface; concentrating defect; ESRD in childhood
Medullary sponge kidneyCystic collecting ducts; innocuous
ADTKDMUC1, UMOD, REN; adult progressive renal failure
NephronophthisisCorticomedullary cysts, normal size; most common pediatric ESRD cause; polyuria, Na wasting; renal-retinal dysplasia; hard to biopsy
Hypoplasia vs dysplasiaHypoplasia = never reached full size; dysplasia = disorganized (primitive mesenchyme and tubules; not pre-neoplastic in kids)
AgenesisUnilateral OK; bilateral lethal
Horseshoe / pelvic kidneyFusion (Turner) / ectopic; may cause infection or a mass
Prune bellyObstruction → hydronephrosis, distended bladder, atrophic abdominal muscle
Potter sequenceBilateral renal disease → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies, limb anomalies; early respiratory death
Ureter duplicationIncomplete (bifid pelvis/ureter) vs complete (two ureters)

Sources: Dr. Walter L. Kemp, MD, PhD, Cystic and Congenital Diseases of the Kidney Parts 1–2 (slides and narration), citing Robbins Basic Pathology (10th ed.) and Becker and Avner (1995). Items tagged "beyond source" are standard teaching points I added.
